overview.title: 📖 Overview: Setting the Calendar and the Counting Procedure
overview.subtitle: Bekhorot 58a–58b
overview.hebrewSource: בְּאֵי זֶה צַד מְעַשְּׂרִין? כּוֹנְסָן לַדִּיר, וְעוֹשֶׂה לָהֶם פֶּתַח קָטָן
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The Gemara explains why animal tithe has three yearly gathering times rather than one: so that plenty of untithed, sellable animals remain available for pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem before each festival. It works out the precise meaning of 'adjacent' (peras) as fifteen days, and traces the different dates given by Rabbi Akiva, ben Azzai, and Rabbi Elazar and Rabbi Shimon to their underlying dispute over when the new year for animal tithe begins — first of Nisan, Elul, or Tishrei. A famous aside has ben Azzai admit that only tradition, not logic, can settle disputes reaching back to the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi. The daf then turns to a new mishna detailing exactly how tithing is performed: animals are herded through a narrow gate one by one, counted to ten, and the tenth is marked with red paint and declared consecrated.

slides.title: 🐑 Why Three Gathering Times, Not One
slides.label: Rabbi Tanḥum's explanation:
slides.text: The three gathering times exist so that animals remain readily available for those making pilgrimage to Jerusalem for each festival. Even though the mishna permits selling or slaughtering animals freely before the gathering date arrives, people generally prefer to perform the mitzva with their property first — tithing — and only then sell or eat the remainder. The gathering time is called a 'goren' (threshing floor) because, just as gathered produce becomes obligated in tithe, animals reaching this point become obligated too.
slides.hebrewSource: כְּדֵי שֶׁתְּהֵא בְּהֵמָה מְצוּיָה לְעוֹלֵי רְגָלִים

slides.title: 📆 Defining 'Adjacent' — and Whose Calendar Applies
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Akiva's fifteen days vs. ben Azzai's fixed dates
rows: 15 days before each festival ('peras' = half of the 30-day pre-Passover study period)
Adar's length varies year to year, so he avoids a fixed calendar date
Holds Adar-before-Nisan is ALWAYS a 29-day month, so he can fix a date
Fewer animals are born in this shorter interval
Waiting the full 15 days would leave no animals left to sell before the festival

slides.title: 🆕 When Does the Animal-Tithe Year Begin?
slides.subtitle: A dispute that reshapes every gathering date

lines.speaker: R' Elazar/Shimon
lines.text: New year is 1 Tishrei — so our third gathering falls on 29 Elul (not 1 Tishrei itself, since that's Rosh Hashanah, a Festival when tithing/painting is forbidden).

lines.speaker: Ben Azzai
lines.text: Since the two views disagree, animals born in Elul are tithed entirely BY THEMSELVES — never combined with either the preceding or following year's animals.

lines.speaker: R' Yochanan
lines.text: Ben Azzai couldn't resolve whose reasoning was stronger because this entire dispute rests on a chain of tradition from the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi — not on logic.

slides.title: 🧄 Ben Azzai's Famous Humility
slides.label: A baraita's report:
slides.text: Ben Azzai said: 'All the Sages of Israel appear to me as unimpressive as garlic peel, except for this bald one' — referring to Rabbi Akiva. Yet even ben Azzai, with all his confidence, could not determine whose reasoning about the new year for animal tithe was more compelling, because the entire matter rested on received tradition rather than logical argument.
slides.hebrewSource: כׇּל חַכְמֵי יִשְׂרָאֵל דּוֹמִין עָלַי כִּקְלִיפַּת הַשּׁוּם חוּץ מִן הַקֵּרֵחַ הַזֶּה

slides.title: 🎨 The Mishna's Tithing Procedure
slides.subtitle: From narrow gate to red paint

steps.content: 1️⃣ Gather the animals into a pen with a narrow opening so only one can exit at a time
2️⃣ Count aloud as each emerges: one, two, three... up to nine
3️⃣ The tenth to emerge is painted with red dye (sikra) and declared: 'This is tithe'

4️⃣ Even without paint or a counting-rod, or if animals were counted while lying down — the tenth is still sanctified after the fact, though if one simply grabbed ten from a hundred without counting, that is NOT valid tithe

callout.label: Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda's exception:
callout.text: He alone holds that even grabbing one animal from ten without any counting still counts as valid tithe — deriving this from teruma's ability to be separated 'by estimate and thought.'

summary.principle: The three annual gathering times for animal tithe exist to keep the market stocked for festival pilgrims, their exact dates hinge on an unresolvable, tradition-based dispute about the new year, and the counting procedure itself — while ideally done with a rod and red paint — is validated after the fact even when performed imperfectly.

flowSteps.content: 🐑 Three gathering times keep untithed animals available for festival pilgrims
📆 'Adjacent' = 15 days (R' Akiva) or fixed calendar dates (ben Azzai), depending on Adar's variable length

columns.content: 🆕 New year: 1 Tishrei (R' Elazar/Shimon) or 1 Elul (R' Meir) — an unresolvable, tradition-rooted dispute
🎨 Counting procedure: narrow gate, count to nine, paint the tenth red — valid even if imperfectly done

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: some halakhic disputes trace back to prophetic tradition itself and cannot be settled by logical argument alone

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Tanḥum, why does animal tithe have three gathering times per year rather than just one?
o: To make the mitzva more difficult
So that untithed, sellable animals remain readily available for pilgrims ascending to Jerusalem before each festival
Because the Torah requires exactly three counts
To match the three daily prayers
quiz.e: The gathering times are timed before each pilgrimage festival specifically so that people will have plenty of non-sacred (untithed) animals available to sell to those coming up to Jerusalem.

quiz.q: Why does ben Azzai fix specific calendar dates (like 29 Adar) for animal-tithe gathering, while Rabbi Akiva instead says '15 days before' each festival?
o: They actually agree completely
Ben Azzai holds Adar immediately before Nisan is always a fixed 29-day month, while Rabbi Akiva holds its length varies, so he avoids naming an exact date
Ben Azzai rejects the whole concept of gathering times
Rabbi Akiva follows a solar calendar instead
quiz.e: Since Rabbi Akiva holds that the length of Adar preceding Nisan can vary between 29 and 30 days, he states the rule relatively ('15 days before Passover') rather than fixing an exact date; ben Azzai holds this Adar is always 29 days, so he can state a fixed date.

quiz.q: According to ben Azzai, why are animals born in the month of Elul tithed entirely by themselves, combined with neither the preceding nor following year's animals?
o: Elul-born animals are considered lesser in value
Because it is uncertain whether the new year for animal tithe begins on 1 Elul (R' Meir) or 1 Tishrei (R' Elazar and R' Shimon)
Because Elul has no gathering time at all
Animals are never born in Elul
quiz.e: Since the tanna'im disagree about whether the new year starts on 1 Elul or 1 Tishrei, ben Azzai rules that Elul-born animals cannot be safely combined with either the prior or following year's animals, so they are tithed as their own separate group.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Yoḥanan, why was ben Azzai — despite his confidence that he outmatched all the Sages except Rabbi Akiva — unable to determine whose reasoning about the new year for animal tithe was correct?
o: He simply didn't study the topic
The entire dispute rested on a received tradition going back to the prophets Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi, not on logical argument
He was afraid of contradicting his teachers
The Temple's destruction made the question moot
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that this particular dispute was transmitted purely as tradition from the last prophets, so it could not be resolved by evaluating whose logical reasoning was more compelling.

quiz.q: In the mishna's tithing procedure, what happens if a person had one hundred animals and simply took ten of them as tithe without individually counting them one by one?
o: This is valid tithe according to everyone
This is NOT valid tithe, according to the first tanna — though Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda disagrees and validates it
The animals become permanently forbidden
This procedure is required by the Torah
quiz.e: The mishna states that taking ten from a hundred (or one from ten) without counting them individually is not valid tithe according to the first tanna, though Rabbi Yosei b'Rabbi Yehuda holds it is still valid, based on a comparison to teruma given 'by estimate and thought.'
